title: NITE 369 — Six-Axis Robotic Arm
summary: Six-axis robotic manipulator built around fully 3D-printed mechanical components and custom compound planetary gearboxes. Distributed control across three RP2040 microcontrollers integrating mechanical design, embedded control, and actuator systems into a low-cost robotic platform.
monoSpec: 6-DOF // Fully 3D-Printed // Compound Planetary Gearboxes // 3x RP2040 Distributed Control

specs.Integration Scope: Mechanical design + embedded control + actuator systems
specs.Design Objective: Low-cost robotic platform for accessible automation

milestones.label: Printed Structural Components
milestones.description: Designed and printed the initial six-axis arm structure with integrated gearbox housings.

milestones.label: Compound Planetary Gearbox Validation
milestones.description: Printed and iterated compound planetary stages; verified reduction ratios and backlash under load.

milestones.label: 3x RP2040 Distributed Control Bring-up
milestones.description: Brought up the three-RP2040 distributed control architecture and integrated motor actuation with embedded control loops.

milestones.label: Integrated Six-Axis Motion Demo
milestones.description: Demonstrated coordinated multi-joint motion on the completed low-cost platform.

problem: Commercial six-axis robot arms are far too expensive for students and makers, and their closed firmware makes customization nearly impossible. This build set out to prove that a fully functional six-axis manipulator can be produced with 3D printing, custom gearboxes, and low-cost microcontrollers.
architecture: The arm uses a distributed control architecture across three RP2040 microcontrollers, each handling a subset of joints and communicating over a shared bus. Mechanical, embedded, and actuator subsystems were developed in parallel to keep everything hosted by the custom printed structure.
mechanical: Every structural link was 3D printed — no machined or purchased arm components. Custom compound planetary gearboxes were designed and printed to provide the required reduction ratios for joint torque, keeping the platform low-cost and prototype-friendly.
electronicsFirmware: Three RP2040 microcontrollers manage joint actuation and feedback across the arm. Embedded control code handles coordinated motion, while each unit drives its assigned motor subsystem from the shared control topology.
control: Each RP2040 runs local joint control; multi-joint coordination is handled across the three-controller distributed architecture, integrating mechanical motion with embedded logic.
results: A working six-axis robotic platform built entirely from printed components, custom compound planetary gearboxes, and three distributed RP2040 controllers — engineered and assembled as a complete low-cost robotic system.

buildLog.entry: Printed first iteration of the base joint housing with integrated gearbox mount.
Iterated compound planetary gearbox print profiles; validated reduction ratio on test rig.
Brought up RP2040 #1 and #2 control nodes; verified joint actuation over the distributed architecture.
Completed six-axis integrated motion demo on the fully printed arm.

title: MARS 369 — Modular Autonomous Robotic Swarm
currentFocus: Docking consensus across the five-unit swarm, and the Avani Dynamics telemetry pipeline
summary: Hexagonal reconfigurable autonomous swarm robotic platform with magnetic latching docks, localized directional IR mesh, and decentralized emergent formation control.
monoSpec: Hexagonal // Electro-Perm Latch // 6-Ch IR Comms // ESP32-S3 Mesh

specs.Form Factor: 115 mm width across flats, 42 mm chassis height
specs.Holding Force: 18.5 N per latch interface (zero continuous power)
specs.Main Processing: Dual-core ESP32-S3 @ 240 MHz with vector neural instructions
specs.Propulsion: Dual N20 micro-geared motors with 334 CPR magnetic encoders
specs.Power Supply: 3.7V 1200 mAh LiPo with onboard USB-C buck-boost charger
specs.Run Time: 3.5 hours active autonomous locomotion and latching

milestones.label: Decentralized Swarm Simulation
milestones.description: Simulated artificial potential fields and lattice self-assembly in Python.

milestones.label: Mechanical Latch Gen-1 Validated
milestones.description: Fabricated self-centering chamfered docking docks with spring-loaded pins.

milestones.label: Zero-Power Electro-Permanent Magnetic Latching
milestones.description: Achieved 18.5N latching with 50ms capacitive discharge pulse; zero power idle.

milestones.label: 5-Unit Swarm Hardware Mesh
milestones.description: Demonstrated directional neighbor discovery and relative bearing sensing via IR.

milestones.label: Autonomous Shape-Shifting & Bridge Formation
milestones.description: 5 units autonomously docked into linear bridge to cross 200mm gap.

milestones.label: Avani Dynamics Formation
milestones.description: Transitioned MARS 369 into flagship commercial IP under startup Avani Dynamics.

problem: Traditional industrial robots are monolithic single-point-of-failure systems. In disaster response, hazardous pipeline inspection, and warehouse logistics, fixed-geometry robots cannot dynamically adapt their physical morphology to squeeze through tight apertures or combine multiple modules to hoist heavy payload structures.
architecture: Each MARS module is fully autonomous with no central coordinator or external camera tracking. Modules discover neighbors through 6 directional IR transceiver pairs arranged hexagonally at 60° increments. Once bearing and ID are exchanged, high-bandwidth data transfers occur over ESP-NOW mesh. Modules execute consensus algorithms using local state vectors to decide cooperative docking formations.
mechanical: The chassis features a 3-layer sandwich construction. The middle layer houses three electro-permanent magnetic (EPM) latches composed of AlNiCo and NdFeB magnet pairs wrapped in 28 AWG magnet wire coils. A brief 50ms pulse switches magnetic polarity, creating 18.5 N holding force with zero ongoing current. Chamfered mechanical guides provide ±8mm and ±12° self-alignment during docking approaches.
electronicsFirmware: Custom hexagonal double-sided PCB serves as both structural bottom deck and electronics motherboard. Circuitry includes dual DRV8837 H-bridge motor drivers, 6-axis BMI270 IMU, battery fuel gauge, capacitive discharge driver for EPM coils, and 6 optically-isolated IR circuits driven by ESP32-S3 hardware LEDC timers.
control: Locomotion is controlled via differential drive kinematic equations with heading regulated by onboard IMU fusion. Flocking and collective behavior use decentralized Artificial Potential Field (APF) equations where virtual attractive forces guide docking candidates while repulsive forces avoid inter-robot collisions.
results: Achieved a 94.2% docking success rate across 80 autonomous indoor trials without external guidance. Demonstrated collective load transport of 4.5 kg using 4 bonded units.

buildLog.entry: Implemented vector field histogram simulation for multi-agent obstacle avoidance.
Wound first batch of 50-turn EPM magnet coils; measured magnetic remanence flip with Hall probe.
Tested pulse capacitor driver; verified 30A 40us discharge without micro-controller brownout.
Outdoor test with 5 units; successfully established peer table in under 800ms upon boot.
Integrated Avani Dynamics telemetry logging protocol for real-time fleet analytics.

title: CAT Autonomous Rover — Caterpillar Autonomous Challenge
summary: Rugged 4WD differential-drive outdoor autonomous rover with centimetre-accurate RTK-GPS, 2D LiDAR SLAM, obstacle avoidance, and mission planner for agricultural mapping.
monoSpec: 4WD // RTK-GPS <2cm // Slamtec A2 LiDAR // ROS2 Nav2 // 4h Battery

specs.Chassis: Welded 6061 aluminum box section with passive rocker suspension
specs.Positioning: u-blox ZED-F9P Multi-band RTK GNSS (< 2 cm accuracy)
specs.Perception: Slamtec RPLiDAR A2M8 (12 m radius, 360° scan @ 10 Hz)
specs.Compute Architecture: Raspberry Pi 4 (ROS2 Humble) + STM32F4 Low-level Motion Hub
specs.Battery Capacity: 24V 20Ah LiFePO4 chemistry with active smart BMS
specs.Operating Range: 4 hours continuous field mapping over rugged terrain
specs.Payload Capacity: 15 kg scientific sensor / soil sampling payload

milestones.label: Rocker Suspension CAD & FEA
milestones.description: Modeled rocker-bogie differential axle to maintain 4-wheel ground contact over 100mm rocks.

milestones.label: Chassis Welding & Drive Train Assembly
milestones.description: TIG-welded aluminum frame and installed sealed planetary gearmotors.

milestones.label: RTK-GPS Centimeter Waypoint Navigation
milestones.description: Achieved waypoint accuracy < 3.5 cm across an open 2-acre agricultural plot.

milestones.label: Full Autonomous Mission Validation
milestones.description: Executed complete 1.8 km autonomous field mapping run with dynamic obstacle avoidance.

problem: The Caterpillar Autonomous Challenge demands a rover that can integrate mechanical hardware, control systems, and onboard electronics into one autonomous platform meeting strict operational requirements. Commercial agri-rover solutions are too costly and closed to adapt to those exact specifications.
architecture: Contributed to a tiered integration architecture for the Caterpillar Autonomous Challenge: a Raspberry Pi 4 running ROS2 handles autonomous navigation, while an STM32F4 manages low-level motion control over CAN bus — combining robotic system integration, embedded electronics, and control systems to meet the challenge's operational requirements.
mechanical: Contributed to the mechanical integration for the Caterpillar Autonomous Challenge rover — chassis, drive layout, and mounting systems designed to meet the challenge's operational and terrain requirements.
electronicsFirmware: Dual 24V 30A BTS7960 motor driver modules, optical quadrature encoders with 1200 CPR, u-blox ANN-MB-00 multi-band GNSS antenna, and isolated DC-DC converters isolating logic circuits from motor back-EMF spikes.
control: Extended Kalman Filter (robot_localization ROS2 node) fuses high-frequency IMU gyro/accel data, wheel encoder odometry, and RTK-GPS fixes. Regulated Pure Pursuit controller drives rover along GPS waypoint sequences with dynamic obstacle re-routing.
results: Contributed to the Caterpillar Autonomous Challenge rover program, integrating mechanical hardware, control systems, and onboard electronics toward the challenge's operational requirements.

buildLog.entry: Calculated wheel torque requirements for 30° gravel incline climb with 15kg payload.
Completed chassis TIG welding; performed structural drop tests from 500mm height.
Configured NTRIP RTCM3 corrections over 4G LTE cellular dongle to achieve RTK-FIX status.
Completed continuous 1.8km field endurance run on local test farm.

title: ScrapX6 — Six-Axis Robot Built from Scrap
summary: Six-axis robotic arm built from salvaged materials and scrap components using NEMA 17 and NEMA 23 stepper motors, TB6600 drivers, and an Arduino Mega. Focused on mechanical assembly, motor control integration, and repurposing discarded components into a functional robotic system. Secured third place at Onfluence 2026.
monoSpec: 6-DOF // Scrap-Built // NEMA 17/23 + TB6600 // Arduino Mega // Onfluence 2026 (3rd Place)

milestones.label: Scrap Sourcing & Mechanical Frame
milestones.description: Salvaged motors, drivers, and structural material; built the initial six-axis frame from reclaimed parts.

milestones.label: NEMA + TB6600 Motor Integration
milestones.description: Wired and configured NEMA 17/23 steppers through TB6600 drivers, integrated with Arduino Mega control logic.

milestones.label: Onfluence 2026 — Third Place
milestones.description: Presented the scrap-built robot at Onfluence 2026 and secured third place.

problem: Robot arms are expensive and often inaccessible to students and makers without funding. ScrapX6 set out to prove a fully functional six-axis robot could be built from salvaged and discarded components rather than purchased kits.
architecture: An Arduino Mega coordinates motor control across NEMA 17 and NEMA 23 steppers driven by TB6600 modules. The system integrates mechanical assembly, motor control, and embedded logic using parts recovered from teardown and scrapyards.
mechanical: Structural components were repurposed from scrap sources and assembled into a six-axis chain, with arm links sized to the salvaged stepper torque envelopes rather than a purchased design.
electronicsFirmware: TB6600 stepper drivers handle NEMA 17/23 current and microstepping, coordinated by the Arduino Mega 2560's multiple hardware timers and serial interfaces.
control: Open-loop stepper choreography with gear-reduction compensation across six axes, tuned against the salvaged motor characteristics.
results: A fully functional six-axis robot built entirely from discarded and salvaged materials, demonstrated live at Onfluence 2026 and awarded third place.

buildLog.entry: Sourced and stripped NEMA 17/23 steppers and TB6600 drivers from donated/scrapped equipment.
Assembled six-axis mechanical frame from scrap; aligned joints under first dead-load test.
Competed at Onfluence 2026 — robot achieved third place.

title: Origin One — First DC-Motor Robot
summary: The first robot I built, during the second year of my diploma: a DC-motor arm carrying a 1 kg payload. The control system is a custom board I designed for this machine, fabricated and soldered by hand on dot board — and it is where I closed my first control loop in hardware.
monoSpec: First Robot // All-DC Drive // 1 kg Payload // Hand-Soldered Dot-Board Control // First Closed Loop

specs.Actuation: DC gear motors driving every joint
specs.Control Electronics: Custom board designed for the complete control system, built on dot board (perfboard) and soldered entirely by hand
specs.Feedback: Two potentiometers — one for the commanded setpoint, one for the actual joint position
specs.Significance: First complete robot build and first closed loop in hardware

milestones.label: Mechanical Frame & Joints
milestones.description: Built the base, arm links and motor mounts by hand around a set of DC gear motors.

milestones.label: Custom Control Board
milestones.description: Designed the single board carrying drive switching, both potentiometer inputs and the controller, then fabricated and soldered it on dot board.

milestones.label: Closed Loop & College Demonstration
milestones.description: Closed the position loop with a setpoint and a joint potentiometer, then presented the finished 1 kg-payload robot at a college function.

problem: A first robot is where theory stops being enough. Building the arm from DC gear motors and a board of my own design meant the mechanics, the drive electronics and the wiring all had to agree with each other. It was also the first time I had to hold a joint at a position rather than switch it on and off.
architecture: DC motors drive every joint, and a single control board designed for this build carries the motor switching, the two potentiometer inputs and the controller. One potentiometer sets the target position, the second is coupled to the joint and reports its actual position, so the controller can close the loop.
mechanical: The arm, base and controller enclosure were built by hand from sheet and box material with salvaged hardware, sized around the DC motors that were available and able to take a 1 kg payload. The joint potentiometers are mechanically coupled to the moving axes.
electronicsFirmware: The control board is dot board — cut, populated and soldered entirely by hand to a design made for this robot: motor switching, both potentiometer inputs and the controller on one board. Debugging it signal by signal was the first real electronics work I did.
control: Closed-loop position control: the setpoint potentiometer sets the target, the joint potentiometer reports the actual position, and the controller drives the DC motor until the difference between them is closed.
results: A working all-DC robot carrying a 1 kg payload with its joints held at commanded positions by closed-loop control, running on a board soldered together by hand — the first machine where I owned the mechanics, the electronics and the wiring end to end.

buildLog.entry: Assembled the base and first arm links around the DC gear motors; checked joint travel by hand.
Finished the custom dot-board control board and brought up the motor channels one at a time.
Tuned the two-potentiometer position loop, tested the 1 kg payload, and photographed the finished robot.

title: Smart Rover — Scrap-Built Robot from Class 8
summary: A rover built in class 8 out of whatever scraps I could find: a PVC-pipe frame lashed with rope over wooden cross members, four salvaged gear motors for wheels, and a three-axis arm on a painted wooden deck. It is driven by hand, and it was shown together with a water sensor, a fire alarm and a non-contact voltage detector carried on the machine.
monoSpec: Class 8 Build // Scrap Parts Only // 4 Gear-Motor Chassis // 3-Axis Arm // Manually Controlled

specs.Frame: PVC pipe ladder frame with wooden cross members, lashed with rope
specs.Drive: Four salvaged gear motors, one per wheel
specs.Arm: Three-axis arm built from scrap timber and aluminium offcuts
specs.Sensor extras: Water sensor, fire alarm, non-contact voltage detector
specs.Materials: Scrap parts only — PVC pipe, timber, salvaged motors, wheels and hardware

milestones.label: Frame and Drive
milestones.description: Lashed the PVC pipe frame over wooden cross members and mounted the four salvaged gear motors and wheels.

milestones.label: Three-Axis Arm
milestones.description: Built the arm from scrap timber and aluminium offcuts and mounted it on the painted wooden deck.

milestones.label: Exhibition Display
milestones.description: Showed the rover with a hand-written specification sheet listing the chassis, the arm and the sensor extras.

problem: The constraint was that nothing could be bought for it: every part had to come out of scraps. The whole design therefore grew around what was already lying around — pipe, timber, motors and wheels — instead of around a drawing.
architecture: Four gear motors drive the wheels of a PVC pipe frame, with a three-axis arm sitting on a wooden deck at the centre of the chassis. The machine is driven by hand, and the sensor extras ride on the same frame as the drive and the arm.
mechanical: The chassis is a ladder of PVC pipe joints, lashed with rope to wooden cross members rather than bolted. The deck is a wooden plate painted in three colours, and the arm is scrap timber and aluminium offcuts pivoting on the same kind of salvaged motor and hardware as the drivetrain.
electronicsFirmware: The drive and arm motors are wired back to a manual control, and the sensor extras — water sensor, fire alarm and non-contact voltage detector — are wired alongside them on the same frame.
control: Manual: the rover is driven and the arm moved by hand from the control wiring, with no autonomous behaviour.
results: A working scrap-built rover that drove and moved its three-axis arm, shown with its hand-written specification sheet.

buildLog.entry: Finished the lashed pipe frame with its four gear motors, wheels and wooden deck, and mounted the three-axis arm on top.
Wired the manual control and the sensor extras, then photographed the rover with its specification sheet at the display.

title: MASR 369 — Minimally Actuated Serial Robot
summary: A serial robot built on the minimally actuated idea: the arm is a chain of hinged links where a joint is either locked or released, so one actuator reconfigures the whole chain instead of every axis carrying its own motor. MASR 369 is the CAD assembly working out that trade — link chain, clamp blocks, base and end plates.
monoSpec: Minimally Actuated Serial Robot // Chain of Hinged Links // Clamped Joints // Fewer Motors Than Axes

specs.Configuration: Serial chain of box-section links, base plate to end plate
specs.Actuation: Fewer motors than joints — joints are clamped or released, so the driven axis repositions the chain
specs.Joint hardware: Circular hinge joints with clamp blocks at each axis
specs.Structure: Box-section links in yellow and black, with base and end plates
specs.Electronics: A mid-chain block mounts the control electronics

milestones.label: Minimally Actuated Concept
milestones.description: Settled the design on a serial chain with fewer actuators than joints, where locking a joint takes that axis out of the driven chain.

milestones.label: Full Chain CAD
milestones.description: Modelled the link chain end to end with hinge joints, clamp blocks, base plate and end plate in one assembly.

milestones.label: Pose Renders
milestones.description: Rendered the assembly upright, folded and extended to show how the chain reconfigures.

problem: A motor per joint is what makes a serial arm heavy, expensive and awkward to wire: every axis adds an actuator, its drive and its cabling. A minimally actuated serial robot takes the other trade — keep the joints, drop most of the motors, and clamp the joints that are not being driven so the remaining actuator can move the chain.
architecture: The robot is a serial chain of hinged links with a base plate at one end and an end plate at the other. Rather than an actuator at every hinge, the joints are clamped or released: locked joints hold their angle, and the driven axis reconfigures the links around them.
mechanical: The links are box-section extrusion in yellow and black, joined by circular hinge joints with clamp blocks at each axis. Base and end plates close the chain at both ends, and a block mid-chain mounts the electronics.
electronicsFirmware: Because the motor count stays low, the drive electronics the chain has to carry stay small; the CAD places them in a block on the chain instead of fanning a drive per axis down the arm.
control: Minimally actuated control: hold the joints that should stay put, release the one being changed, and drive the powered axis so the end plate walks through a sequence of poses without an actuator at every joint.
results: A complete CAD assembly of a minimally actuated serial robot — link chain, clamp blocks, base and end plates and the mid-chain electronics block — shown both folded and extended.

buildLog.entry: Assembled the link chain in CAD and worked out the clamp block at each hinge.
Rendered the upright, folded and extended poses of the assembly.
